Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The two liver metastases are limited in number (2), size (<3 cm), and location (segments II and V) such that a segmental (non‑major) hepatectomy would leave at least two contiguous hepatic segments with adequate inflow, outflow and biliary drainage. The anticipated future liver remnant exceeds the 20‑30 % functional threshold. No extra‑hepatic disease is present. The primary colon lesion is symptomatic and can be addressed surgically at the same time, making an immediate combined resection technically feasible.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT with volumetry) to confirm lesion size, relationship to vascular structures and calculate FLR.  
   • Baseline labs: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available, CEA trend.  
   • Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary fitness for combined surgery.  

2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   • Left‑sided colon cancer: standard oncologic left hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy and primary anastomosis (or diverting stoma if intra‑operative concern).  
   • Liver: anatomical segmental resections of segment II and segment V using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins; aim for R0 (≥1 mm) resection.  
   • No need for portal vein embolization or two‑stage approach given limited hepatic resection.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   • Start adjuvant chemotherapy within 6‑8 weeks after recovery (preferably 6 months).  
   • Preferred regimen: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type and left‑sided, provided no contraindication.  
   • Monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  

4. Consideration of targeted therapy/clinical trial  
   • If high‑risk features (elevated CEA, T4 primary, node‑positive) are confirmed on pathology, discuss addition of adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based regimen with or without biologic per multidisciplinary consensus.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Detailed liver function assessment (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance) and volumetric calculation of future liver remnant.  
• Performance status (ECOG) and cardiopulmonary evaluation to confirm fitness for combined surgery.  
• Pathologic staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, nodal status) after resection, which will influence adjuvant therapy intensity.  
• Baseline renal function and neuropathy status to guide chemotherapy choice.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI can be removed with a wedge or segmental resection while preserving >2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease identified on FDG‑PET; imaging suggests isolated liver involvement.  
- The primary tumor is located in the right colon and can be addressed with a standard right hemicolectomy.  
- No reported comorbidities or hepatic dysfunction that would preclude major abdominal surgery.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Simultaneous (combined) resection: perform right hemicolectomy together with a limited hepatic resection (segment VI wedge/segmentectomy) in the same operative session. This approach is supported when the liver lesion is small, peripheral, and does not require a major hepatectomy.  
- Pre‑operative work‑up: obtain high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to confirm absence of additional occult lesions and to plan the hepatic transection margin (aim ≥1 mm, preferably ≥5 mm). Verify liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance or volumetry if any concern about FLR.  
- Post‑operative systemic therapy: start adjuvant chemotherapy within 6‑8 weeks after surgery. Recommended regimen: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPEOX) ± bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents not indicated).  
- Surveillance: CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen (or MRI liver) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
- Multidisciplinary follow‑up: review pathology (T‑stage, N‑status, margin status) to decide on need for further adjuvant therapy (e.g., oxaliplatin‑based regimen if high‑risk features).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and detailed comorbidity profile.  
- Baseline liver function tests and quantitative future liver remnant volume (if any concern).  
- Pathologic staging of the primary tumor (T and N status) and exact margin status after resection.  
- Details on any pre‑existing hepatic steatosis or fibrosis that could affect postoperative liver regeneration.  
- Information on patient’s preferences regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the solitary 1.8 cm metastasis in segment III is technically resectable with a limited segmentectomy and would leave an adequate future liver remnant. However, curative treatment of the upper rectal primary requires pre‑operative short‑course radiotherapy (and, per standard practice, a restaging scan to confirm that the liver lesion remains resectable after radiotherapy). Until that radiotherapy and confirmatory imaging are completed, definitive surgery cannot be performed.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Short‑course pre‑operative radiotherapy for the rectal primary (5 × 5 Gy over 1 week).  
2. Restaging 4–6 weeks after RT with pelvic MRI and liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to verify:  
   - No progression of the liver metastasis,  
   - No new extra‑hepatic disease (especially lung or peritoneal).  
3. Multidisciplinary decision on peri‑operative systemic therapy:  
   - Because the primary is T3N1 and the patient is RAS‑wild‑type, a short course (2–3 cycles) of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) after radiotherapy can be offered to assess tumor biology and treat micrometastatic disease.  
   - If imaging after chemotherapy still shows a solitary, stable lesion, proceed to surgery.  
4. Surgical phase – simultaneous resection (performed 2–3 weeks after the last chemotherapy cycle, provided the patient’s performance status remains adequate):  
   - Laparoscopic low anterior resection (LAR) of the upper rectal tumor with total mesorectal excision; creation of a defunctioning loop ileostomy is optional based on intra‑operative assessment.  
   - Laparoscopic or open segment III segmentectomy (or wedge resection) achieving R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm no additional occult lesions.  
   - Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments and ensure FLR > 30 % (automatically satisfied after removal of segment III).  
5. Post‑operative management:  
   - Pathology‑driven adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months systemic therapy (including any pre‑operative cycles).  
   - If the primary pathology shows high‑risk features (e.g., positive margins, extramural vascular invasion), consider intensifying adjuvant therapy (e.g., addition of biologic agent).  
   - Ileostomy reversal after 8–10 weeks, provided anastomotic healing is confirmed.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
The case lacks several pieces of information that are essential for a definitive plan:  
- Comprehensive staging of the chest (CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR calculation) to confirm that removal of segment III leaves an adequate remnant.  
- Baseline performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary reserve to gauge tolerance of combined surgery.  
- Details of any comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes) that could influence timing or choice of simultaneous versus staged resection.  
- Results of baseline pelvic MRI regarding circumferential resection margin (CRM) and distance from mesorectal fascia, which may affect the need for a more extensive rectal resection or influence the decision to place a protective stoma.  

These data should be obtained before finalizing the treatment schedule.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Three hepatic metastases (2‑3 cm) in segments IV, V and VI with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no vascular invasion → technically amenable to non‑anatomic or limited anatomical resection while preserving ≥30 % future liver remnant.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease reported; KRAS mutation and high CEA are adverse prognostic markers but do not preclude curative surgery.  
- MDT already judged the lesions “primarily resectable” and a “simple liver surgery possible,” supporting immediate surgical feasibility provided the patient’s physiological reserve is adequate.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Full performance status (ECOG/ASA), cardiopulmonary assessment, liver function tests, and volumetric CT/MRI to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy).  
   - Staging of the primary tumour (T‑stage, nodal status) and chest imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude occult pulmonary metastases.  
2. Surgical plan (if fitness confirmed)  
   - Simultaneous resection is preferred in fit patients:  
     • Segmental colectomy for the transverse colon cancer with oncologic margins (≥ 1 mm circumferential).  
     • Liver‑first approach: non‑anatomic wedge resections or limited segmentectomy of segments IV, V and VI achieving R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to verify margins and exclude additional lesions.  
   - Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   - If intra‑operative assessment reveals inadequate FLR, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a staged two‑step hepatectomy.  
3. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Post‑operative 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) ± anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) given KRAS‑mutated, synchronous disease and high pre‑operative CEA.  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months; imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  
4. Alternative sequencing (if patient not fit for combined operation)  
   - Stage the procedures: either (a) liver resection first (to secure curative intent for metastases) followed by delayed colectomy, or (b) primary tumour resection first if obstruction/bleeding risk, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy bridging to liver surgery.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s ECOG/ASA performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiac, pulmonary, renal).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and quantitative FLR calculation.  
- Exact T‑stage and N‑stage of the transverse colon tumour.  
- Results of chest CT or PET‑CT to definitively rule out pulmonary metastases.  
- MSI/MMR status (relevant for immunotherapy considerations).  
- Planned peri‑operative chemotherapy regimen and timing (if any) before surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The four liver metastases are peripheral (segments II, III, V, VIII), each ≤ 3 cm, with no vascular invasion or extra‑hepatic disease. Technical criteria for colorectal liver metastasis resection (preservation of ≥ 2 contiguous segments, adequate inflow/outflow/biliary drainage and an FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) can be satisfied with either multiple non‑anatomic wedge resections or limited segmentectomies. Current literature confirms that ≤ 4 peripheral lesions are routinely resectable without pre‑operative down‑staging, so surgery can be offered immediately.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative confirmation  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or CT‑MRI fusion) to verify that no additional lesions are present and to perform volumetric analysis of the future liver remnant.  
   • Standard pre‑operative work‑up: cardiopulmonary assessment, liver function tests, ECOG status, nutritional assessment.  

2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   • Primary tumor – Laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (aim for R0, T3N1).  
   • Liver metastases – Perform parenchymal‑sparing resections:  
     – Segment II/III wedge or segmentectomy (left lateral) for the two left‑lobe lesions.  
     – Segment V and VIII wedge resections (or limited segmentectomies) for the right‑lobe lesions.  
   • Aim for negative microscopic margins (≥ 1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous segments and an FLR ≥ 30 % (expected > 55 % given the peripheral nature of the lesions).  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion count and location; use Pringle maneuver only if needed, with limited ischemia time.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   • Given RAS‑wild‑type disease, N1 nodal status and four metastases, administer adjuvant FOLFOX (6 cycles) combined with cetuximab (or panitumumab) to target micrometastatic disease.  
   • If postoperative pathology shows favorable response and no high‑risk features, consider completing 12 cycles total (pre‑operative 0, post‑operative 6–12).  

4. Surveillance  
   • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.  

5. Alternative pathway (if intra‑operative FLR < 30 % or unexpected vascular involvement)  
   • Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) followed by staged hepatectomy, or a two‑stage liver resection with interval systemic therapy.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
The case lacks several pieces of information that are essential for a fully individualized plan:  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, indocyanine‑green clearance).  
- Volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
- Performance status / ASA classification and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, diabetes).  
- Details on whether the primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) that might influence timing of colectomy.  
- Results of pre‑operative chest imaging to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases.  

These data should be obtained before finalizing the operative schedule.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

The two hepatic lesions (3 cm in segment II and 4 cm in segment IVa) can be removed with negative margins while preserving the middle hepatic vein and leaving more than the required 30 % future liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease has been reported. From a technical standpoint the case meets all current criteria for an R0 liver resection (adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage and FLR). Therefore the metastases are resectable without the need for pre‑operative down‑staging.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Baseline assessment – Obtain full pre‑operative work‑up:  
   • ECOG/ASA performance status, cardiopulmonary evaluation, liver function tests, and volumetric CT‑based FLR calculation.  
   • Chest CT or PET‑CT to confirm absence of pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  

2. Systemic therapy (peri‑operative) – Because the primary tumour is T4 N2 (high‑risk) and KRAS‑mutated, give 6 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF).  
   • Goal: treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumour biology, and potentially improve disease‑free survival (EORTC 40983 data).  
   • Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI) after chemotherapy to confirm that the lesions have not progressed and that the FLR remains adequate.  

3. Surgical sequencing – Two acceptable approaches, choose based on patient fitness and primary‑tumour symptoms:  

   a. Simultaneous resection (if fit and no obstruction)  
   • Right hemicolectomy with en‑bloc mesocolic excision (aim for R0).  
   • Left lateral segmentectomy (segments II‑III) plus non‑anatomic wedge of segment IVa, preserving the middle hepatic vein.  
   • Benefits: single operative episode, earlier control of both sites, reduced total hospital stay.  

   b. Staged (liver‑first) strategy – preferred when the primary tumour is asymptomatic but the liver disease is considered the limiting factor.  
   • First operation: liver resection as described above (segment II‑III + segment IVa wedge).  
   • Recovery (≈4–6 weeks), then right hemicolectomy.  
   • Rationale: avoids potential delay of liver resection while the patient recovers from bowel surgery; aligns with literature that liver‑first can prevent loss of resectability during postoperative recovery.  

4. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy – Complete a total of 12 cycles of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative 6 cycles). If the patient received bevacizumab pre‑operatively, resume it post‑operatively after wound healing (≥6 weeks).  

5. Surveillance – CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

A reliable final plan requires the following essential information that has not been provided:  

- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and quantitative FLR volume.  
- Chest imaging to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Symptoms or obstruction related to the right‑sided primary tumour (e.g., bleeding, perforation).  
- Details of any prior neoadjuvant therapy already given to the primary tumour.  

These data are needed to confirm fitness for major combined surgery and to finalize the sequencing (simultaneous vs staged).

Case_Content:
Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the hepatic disease meets technical criteria for R0 resection (three lesions ≤2 cm, confined to the right liver, allowing segmental or wedge resections with an adequate future liver remnant). However, definitive curative surgery cannot be performed immediately because the rectal primary requires short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (and possibly a brief interval) before a safe oncologic resection. Completion of the radiotherapy (and its associated waiting period) is a prerequisite to proceeding with either a simultaneous or staged liver‑plus‑rectal operation.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) for the upper‑rectal T3N0 tumor.  
• During the 1‑2 week interval after radiotherapy, obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with volumetry to confirm FLR (>30 % of total liver volume) and to rule out occult lesions.  
• Systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody, given RAS‑wild type) can be administered either:  
   – Neoadjuvantly (2–3 cycles) during the radiotherapy‑to‑surgery interval to assess tumor biology and further downsize any microscopic disease, or  
   – Postoperatively as adjuvant therapy after both resections, depending on patient tolerance and multidisciplinary consensus.  
• Surgical sequence (chosen after radiotherapy and imaging review):  
   1. Liver‑first option – perform a limited right‑posterior hepatectomy (segmental/wedge resections of segments VI‑VIII) preserving a robust left‑lobe FLR; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm complete clearance.  
   2. Four to six weeks later, undertake low‑anterior resection (or anterior resection) of the rectal primary with a protective loop ileostomy, given the recent radiotherapy.  
   – If the operative risk is deemed low and the patient is fit, a simultaneous approach (combined liver resection and low‑anterior resection) can be considered after radiotherapy, provided the anticipated liver remnant remains ≥30 % and operative time is acceptable.  
• Pathology review for margin status (aim R0) and postoperative liver function monitoring.  
• Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (total 6 months of peri‑operative FOLFOX ± cetuximab) to address micrometastatic disease.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and pelvis every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Detailed liver volumetry (future liver remnant percentage).  
• High‑resolution liver MRI to exclude sub‑centimeter lesions not seen on CT.  
• Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets).  
• Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and sphincter involvement to confirm feasibility of low‑anterior resection versus more extensive pelvic surgery.  
• Patient’s preference regarding timing of surgeries and willingness to receive peri‑operative chemotherapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The patient has a solitary 2.7 cm metastasis in segment IVb, an anatomically favorable location that can be removed with a wedge resection or segmentectomy while preserving a ≥30 % future liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, and the primary tumour is left‑sided. Assuming adequate performance status and liver function (which are typical in a hypertensive 70‑year‑old without known hepatic disease), the lesion meets both technical and oncological criteria for immediate curative surgery without the need for down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete pre‑operative staging  
  – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary agent to confirm size, margins and FLR volume.  
  – Chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  
  – Full colonoscopic assessment and pathology of the primary (T/N stage).  
  – Baseline labs: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, CA‑19‑9, full blood count, renal function.  

• Multidisciplinary fitness assessment  
  – ECOG/ASA classification, cardiopulmonary evaluation, assessment of hypertension control.  

• Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
  – Left‑sided colectomy (segmental or left hemicolectomy) with primary anastomosis, performed either open or laparoscopically according to surgeon expertise.  
  – Segment IVb resection (segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge) aiming for R0 margin (≥1 cm when feasible, ≤5 mm acceptable if negative intra‑operative frozen section).  
  – Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
  – Ensure FLR ≥30 % (or liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio >0.5 %).  

• Post‑operative management  
  – Standard enhanced recovery pathway, monitor liver function, early mobilization, and CEA trend.  
  – Pathology review for margin status, lymph‑node involvement, vascular/lymphatic invasion.  

• Adjuvant systemic therapy (recommended)  
  – Because the disease is biologically favorable (left‑sided, BRAF‑wt, MSS, solitary lesion) and the patient is fit, start adjuvant FOLFOX (or CAPOX) for 6 months; add anti‑EGFR (cetuximab or panitumumab) if RAS is wild‑type.  
  – If postoperative pathology shows high‑risk features (e.g., N‑positive nodes, lymph‑vascular invasion), consider extending to 12 months or adding a biologic per current ESMO guidelines.  

• Surveillance  
  – CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
  – Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually up to 5 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
A definitive recommendation would be strengthened by the following essential information that is not provided:  
- Performance status (ECOG) and ASA classification.  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
- Primary tumour staging (T stage, N stage, presence of lymph‑node metastasis).  
- RAS mutation status (KRAS/NRAS) to guide anti‑EGFR use.  
- Cardiopulmonary assessment results (e.g., echocardiogram, pulmonary function) to confirm operative fitness.  
- Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.  

If any of these parameters reveal significant impairment (e.g., poor liver reserve, high operative risk, or unfavorable primary‑tumour stage), the plan may need to be modified accordingly.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis located in segment IVb, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion is anatomically favorable for a a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary metastasis with favorable anatomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm the relationship of the lesion to segment IVb vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology, however the KRAS status is unknown.
• BRAF wild-type and MSS status do not modify the surgical indication.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT. 

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment IVb wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures (Wisneski et al.; Kim et al.) However, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. K-Ras status, grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor with two contiguous liver metastases in segment VI (2.1 and 2.4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 180 ng/mL, KRAS mutation.
MDT Discussion: Limited and accessible liver involvement, no indication for upfront chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Two liver metastases are small (2.1 cm and 2.4 cm), located in the same segment (VI) and can be removed with a non‑anatomic wedge or segmentectomy, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and leaving a future liver remnant well above the 30 % threshold.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on the staging CT.  
- The primary sigmoid lesion is T3N1 and amenable to standard oncologic resection with primary anastomosis.  
- The MDT already concluded that there is “limited and accessible liver involvement, no indication for upfront chemotherapy,” supporting immediate surgical cure.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Stage 1 (Surgery – simultaneous approach)  
  • Perform a laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy and primary anastomosis.  
  • Perform a limited hepatic resection (segment VI wedge/segmentectomy) aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm acceptable).  
  • Sequence can be liver resection first followed by colon resection to minimize tumor spillage; both procedures can be completed in the same operative session because the liver resection is minor.  

- Stage 2 (Pathology and risk assessment)  
  • Confirm R0 resection of both sites, assess number of positive nodes, margin status, and tumor grade.  
  • Record KRAS‑mutated status (already known) and postoperative CEA level.  

- Stage 3 (Adjuvant systemic therapy)  
  • Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks after recovery, preferably a 6‑month course of FOLFOX or CAPOX (oxaliplatin‑based) – anti‑EGFR agents are not indicated because of KRAS mutation.  
  • Consider adding bevacizumab only in the context of a clinical trial, as routine addition has not shown survival benefit in the adjuvant setting.  

- Stage 4 (Surveillance)  
  • CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
  • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the chest, abdomen and pelvis every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant to confirm adequacy.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary reserve to ensure tolerance of combined surgery.  
- Detailed imaging of the colon primary (extent of mesorectal involvement, if any) to confirm that a low‑risk colorectal resection is feasible.  
- Post‑operative pathology details (margin width, lymph‑node count) that will refine adjuvant therapy decisions.

Case_Content:
Woman, 65 years old, simultaneous discovery of a right colon adenocarcinoma and a 3 cm liver metastasis in segment VII at the abdominal CT scan CEA 70 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep but resectable metastasis, discussion of simultaneous versus sequential surgery.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: • Single liver lesion, 3 cm, located in segment VII – amenable to a non‑anatomic wedge or formal segmentectomy with preservation of >30 % functional liver remnant. • No reported extra‑hepatic disease, vascular invasion, or major biliary involvement. • Primary tumour is in the right colon; a standard right hemicolectomy is a low‑complexity bowel operation. • Patient age (65) and RAS wild‑type status do not preclude surgery. In the absence of contraindicating comorbidities or insufficient future liver remnant, the disease meets current criteria for immediate curative resection.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Baseline work‑up: complete contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases; liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast for precise volumetry; laboratory panel (bilirubin, INR, albumin, liver enzymes, CA 19‑9); assessment of performance status and comorbidities (ASA, cardiac/pulmonary reserve).  
• Multidisciplinary decision: proceed with a simultaneous resection because (a) the liver operation is limited (segment VII) and (b) the primary tumour is right‑sided and asymptomatic. This approach shortens overall treatment time, avoids two separate major operations, and is supported by multiple series (Thelen 2007; Weber 2003; Reddy 2007) showing comparable morbidity and survival to staged procedures when the hepatic resection is minor.  
• Peri‑operative systemic therapy: administer 2–3 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± bevacizumab as a “test‑of‑time” to confirm disease biology and to treat micrometastatic disease. Imaging after chemotherapy should confirm that the liver lesion remains resectable and that no new lesions have appeared.  
• Operative plan (within 4–6 weeks of completing chemotherapy):  
   – Right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis (or ileocolic anastomosis) performed first to secure low central venous pressure and minimise intra‑hepatic bleeding.  
   – Segment VII non‑anatomic wedge or formal segmentectomy with negative (≥1 mm) margin; intra‑operative ultrasound to verify margins and assess for additional occult lesions.  
   – No need for portal vein embolisation given the small volume of liver to be removed.  
• Post‑operative care: early mobilization, resume oral intake, monitor liver function.  
• Adjuvant systemic therapy: complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (add additional cycles post‑op to reach 6 months) as per EORTC 40983 protocol, given the elevated pre‑operative CEA (70 ng/mL) and synchronous presentation.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT chest/abdomen every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
• Comprehensive comorbidity assessment (ASA class, cardiac/pulmonary reserve, performance status).  
• Full staging of the primary tumour (T‑stage, N‑stage, lymphovascular/perineural invasion).  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest imaging, possible PET‑CT).  
• Assessment of vascular anatomy around segment VII (proximity to hepatic veins or portal branches) to plan resection margin.  
If any of these items are unavailable, a definitive recommendation cannot be fully validated.

• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles).

Case_Content:
Man, 53 years old, T3N0M1 sigmoid colon tumor, multiple metastases limited to the left lobe (three lesions 1-2.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 150 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, left liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Three liver metastases (1–2.5 cm) are confined to the left hepatic lobe; a left lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) or left hepatectomy can remove all lesions while preserving the right liver (>50 % of total volume).  
- No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease; the primary sigmoid tumour is T3N0 and amenable to standard oncologic resection.  
- KRAS mutation and elevated CEA do not affect the technical feasibility of liver resection.  
- Assuming adequate liver function and acceptable performance status, the disease meets the technical criteria of (a) complete R0 removal, (b) preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow, and (c) an FLR >30 % – therefore surgery can be offered immediately without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm functional reserve.  
   - Volumetric CT or MRI to quantify future liver remnant (target ≥30 % for normal liver).  
   - Baseline performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary assessment.  
2. Surgical plan  
   - Simultaneous resection (preferred) because the hepatic resection is limited and the colorectal primary is in the sigmoid colon:  
     • Laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (D3).  
     • Left lateral sectionectomy (or left hepatectomy if required) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion count and margins; aim for R0 (≥1 mm) resection.  
   - If intra‑operative findings reveal additional occult liver lesions, consider intra‑operative ablation (RFA/SBRT) to achieve complete disease clearance.  
3. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Start adjuvant chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks after surgery: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) given KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   - Planned duration: 6 months (12 cycles).  
   - Monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
4. Multidisciplinary follow‑up  
   - Review pathology (margin status, number of nodes, molecular profile).  
   - If margins are R1 or high‑risk features (e.g., poor response to adjuvant therapy), discuss enrollment in clinical trials or consider postoperative radiotherapy to the liver bed (rare).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin) and quantitative FLR measurement.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary, diabetes).  
- Detailed imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or high‑resolution CT) to rule out sub‑centimeter lesions not seen on the initial CT.  
- Molecular profile beyond KRAS (BRAF, MSI/dMMR) which may influence adjuvant therapy choices.  
- Baseline cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., VO₂ max or stress test) to confirm fitness for combined abdominal surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases confined to the left lobe (segments II/III/IV), measuring 1–2.5 cm, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Case_Content:
Woman, 66 years old, high rectal T3N1 cancer with a single 1.5 cm metastasis in segment II at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 50 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Peripheral resectable metastasis, possibility of combined surgery after pelvic treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the hepatic lesion (1.5 cm in segment II) is technically amenable to R0 resection with an adequate future liver remnant. However, curative intent surgery cannot be performed immediately because the rectal primary (high T3) requires neoadjuvant pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± chemoradiation) before definitive resection. The prerequisite action is completion of neoadjuvant therapy for the rectal tumor (or short‑course radiotherapy followed by timely surgery) prior to any hepatic or combined operation.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate neoadjuvant treatment for the rectal primary:  
   – Preferred option: long‑course chemoradiation (50.4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent capecitabine or 5‑FU) followed by a 6‑8 week interval;  
   – Alternative for fit patients: short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) with surgery scheduled within 1–2 weeks, allowing simultaneous liver resection.  
• During the neoadjuvant interval, give systemic chemotherapy aimed at the metastatic disease (e.g., 4–6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX). RAS‑wild‑type status permits addition of an anti‑EGFR agent (cetuximab) if a more aggressive systemic approach is desired.  
• Restage after chemoradiation (or after short‑course RT): repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to confirm stability of the segment II metastasis, assess FLR volume, and exclude new lesions; repeat pelvic MRI to verify tumor response and mesorectal fascia status; obtain chest imaging to rule out occult pulmonary disease; re‑measure CEA.  
• Surgical sequencing (choose one based on multidisciplinary consensus and patient fitness):  
   – Liver‑first approach: perform a laparoscopic or open left lateral segmentectomy (non‑anatomic wedge or segmentectomy) with R0 margins, preserving ≥30 % FLR. After recovery (≈4–6 weeks) proceed to total mesorectal excision (TME) with a protective loop ileostomy if indicated.  
   – Simultaneous approach (if short‑course RT is used and patient is low‑risk): combine left lateral segmentectomy with low anterior resection/TME in a single operation, using minimally invasive techniques when feasible.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: complete a total of 6 months peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (including any pre‑operative cycles) to address micrometastatic disease. Consider adding a short course of postoperative radiotherapy boost if the pathological response of the rectal tumor is suboptimal.  
• Follow‑up: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen and chest CT annually for at least 5 years, or sooner if clinical suspicion arises.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Detailed liver volumetry (future liver remnant percentage) and hepatic function tests (bilirubin, INR, ICG clearance if available).  
• Performance status/ECOG and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve, ASA classification).  
• High‑resolution pelvic MRI findings (mesorectal fascia involvement, distance to sphincter, nodal status).  
• Chest imaging results (CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
• Baseline tumor markers beyond CEA (e.g., CA 19‑9) if available.  
• Patient’s preference regarding sequencing (liver‑first vs. simultaneous) and willingness for minimally invasive surgery.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left T4aN2 colon cancer, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Max size 3.8 cm. CEA 330 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Limited liver involvement, potentially curative upfront.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The three metastases are ≤ 4 cm, located in segments IV, V and VIII, which can be removed with non‑anatomical or limited anatomical resections while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and an estimated future liver remnant > 30 % (the lesions are small and limited in number). No extra‑hepatic disease is reported. Technical criteria (adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage) are satisfied, and there is no indication of vascular invasion. Therefore the hepatic disease meets current oncologic and technical definitions of resectability and can be addressed without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Obtain liver volumetry (CT‑based or MRI) to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy).  
   – Full staging (chest CT, PET‑CT if indicated) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Assess performance status, cardiopulmonary reserve, and liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin).  

• Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but advised)  
   – Because of high‑risk primary features (T4a, N2, KRAS‑mutated, CEA 330 ng/mL), give 3 – 4 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab.  
   – Re‑image after chemotherapy to confirm disease stability or response; progression would defer surgery.  

• Surgical sequencing (most appropriate for this presentation)  
   – Simultaneous resection: perform a left‑sided colectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) combined with limited hepatic resections (segment IV, segment V and segment VIII wedge/segmentectomies) in the same operative session.  
   – Rationale: liver resections are minor (no major hepatectomy), operative time and morbidity are acceptable, and simultaneous surgery avoids a second laparotomy and potential disease progression while the primary is still resectable.  

• Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy (including the pre‑operative cycles).  
   – Consider adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based regimen; anti‑VEGF continuation is optional based on tolerance.  
   – Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
A reliable final plan would benefit from the following essential information that is not provided:  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT/MRI volumetry).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, diabetes).  
- Detailed imaging of the primary tumor to confirm resectability margins and any adjacent organ involvement.  
- Confirmation that there is no occult extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., PET‑CT or high‑resolution chest CT).  

These data should be obtained before finalizing the operative schedule.

Woman, 74 years old, right T3N0 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments III and VI (2.2 and 3 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 88 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Anatomically accessible metastases, indication for primary surgery.
Response:

- Two liver metastases (2.2 cm in segment III, 3 cm in segment VI) are small, anatomically accessible and amenable to segmental resection.  
- Technical criteria (ability to achieve R0 margins, preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments, adequate inflow/outflow) appear satisfied.  
- Definitive classification requires confirmation that the future liver remnant (FLR) will be ≥30 % of total liver volume (or FLR/body‑weight ratio > 0.5). This information is not provided; therefore resection cannot be declared upfront.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, and BRAF wild‑type status is favorable, but performance status, comorbidities and baseline liver function are unknown and could also preclude surgery.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain ECOG/ASA score, detailed cardiopulmonary assessment, liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin), and volumetric imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) to calculate FLR.  
   - Verify RAS mutation status and MSI/dMMR status (both influence systemic therapy choice).  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but advisable)  
   - Because the disease is synchronous, CEA is elevated (88 ng/mL) and the patient is elderly, give a short course (3–4 cycles) of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (if RAS wild‑type) to assess tumor biology (“proof of time”) and treat micrometastatic disease.  
   - Re‑stage with imaging after chemotherapy to confirm that lesions remain resectable and that FLR is still adequate.  

3. Surgical sequencing  
   - If the patient is fit and FLR is sufficient, proceed with a simultaneous operation: right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with lymphadenectomy) combined with segmental resections of segment III and segment VI (non‑anatomic or anatomical segmentectomy) aiming for R0 margins.

4. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative cycles). Adjust regimen based on postoperative pathology (margin status, nodal status, RAS/BRAF).  

5. Surveillance  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of liver, chest CT) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually up to 5 years.

- ECOG performance status / ASA classification.  
- Detailed comorbidity profile (cardiac, pulmonary, renal).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- RAS mutation status and MSI/dMMR status.  
- Histologic grade of the primary tumor.  
- Patient’s preference regarding surgical timing and willingness for chemotherapy.

   – Because the hepatic resection required is limited (segment V), a simultaneous approach is safe and reduces overall treatment time, provided the patient’s ASA I–II status and cardiopulmonary reserve are acceptable.

- Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and MRI assessment of mesorectal fascia involvement.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, hepatic function).  
- Baseline liver function tests and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
- Presence or absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease on chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Details of any prior neoadjuvant therapy already administered.  

If any of these data are unavailable, they must be obtained before finalizing the surgical sequence.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the current disease burden (seven bilobar lesions, some in contact with the right portal branch) makes an R0 liver resection impossible without prior intervention. A specific prerequisite is required: conversion systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab) to downsize the metastases and/or induce sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) hypertrophy (potentially with portal vein embolisation) before a curative‑intent hepatectomy can be planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate conversion chemotherapy with FOLFOX + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR antibodies).  
 – Give 3–6 cycles; assess tumour response after every 2–3 cycles using contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI and RECIST criteria.  
• Re‑evaluate liver anatomy after chemotherapy:  
 – Measure FLR (CT volumetry). If FLR < 30 % (or < 0.5 % body‑weight ratio), schedule portal vein embolisation (PVE) to induce hypertrophy.  
 – If vascular involvement persists, consider vascular reconstruction or a staged approach (two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS) to achieve clear margins while preserving inflow/outflow.  
• Primary colon tumour:  
 – Because the primary is T4aN2, plan definitive oncologic resection (right hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
 – If the colon tumour is symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding) or at high risk of complications, perform it first; otherwise, after confirming hepatic down‑staging, a simultaneous resection can be considered in a fit patient.  
• Once imaging shows all liver lesions amenable to R0 resection and an adequate FLR, proceed to hepatic surgery:  
 – Goal: complete removal of all seven metastases with ≥1 mm negative margin, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
 – Preferred operative plan: right hepatectomy (or extended right hepatectomy) combined with non‑anatomic wedge resections of remaining lesions; if FLR remains marginal, execute the second stage after hypertrophy.  
• Post‑operative management:  
 – Pathology‑driven adjuvant chemotherapy (continue FOLFOX‑based regimen for 6 months if tolerated).  
 – Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and quantitative FLR assessment.  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, bone) on full staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET‑CT).  
• Details of the primary tumour’s resectability (obstruction, perforation) and whether it has already been resected.  
• Exact size and spatial relationship of each liver lesion to major vessels (right hepatic vein, middle hepatic vein, portal branches) to plan vascular control or reconstruction.  
• Planned timing between the last dose of bevacizumab and surgery (generally 6–8 weeks).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven bilobar liver metastases (1–4 cm) associated with vascular contact with the right portal branch and no reported extrahepatic disease. The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and portal contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant unlikely with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (520 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX + bevacizumab.

Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the case requires a prerequisite step (completion of neoadjuvant chemotherapy with re‑imaging and volumetric assessment) before a definitive surgical plan can be made. At present the four bilobar lesions (segments II, III, VI, VIII) include one abutting the right hepatic vein, and no quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) data are available. Consequently a curative‑intent liver resection cannot be declared upfront.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy  
  • Begin a 4‑cycle neoadjuvant regimen with a doublet or triplet oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) plus an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type.  
  • Monitor CEA after each cycle; aim for a ≥50 % decline and radiologic response on contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI.  

- Restaging after 4 cycles  
  • Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and obtain a volumetric CT scan to calculate FLR (target ≥30 % of total liver volume, ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
  • Re‑measure each metastasis; note any change in the lesion contacting the right hepatic vein.  

- Decision point based on restaging  
  1. If FLR is adequate and all lesions can be cleared with negative (R0) margins – proceed to a single‑stage, parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy combined with definitive sigmoid resection (low anterior resection or Hartmann’s, according to intra‑colonic disease).  
     - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to guide non‑anatomic wedge resections of segments II, III, VI, VIII.  
     - For the lesion adherent to the right hepatic vein, consider:  
        a marginal (R1) vascular resection if the contact is <25 % of the vein circumference and reconstruction is feasible, or  
        en‑bloc resection of the involved vein segment with primary repair or graft if oncologic safety demands.  
  2. If FLR is insufficient or a safe margin cannot be achieved – adopt a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) strategy:  
     - Stage 1: Left lateral (segments II‑III) non‑anatomic resection of the left‑side lesions; perform right portal vein embolization (or portal vein ligation) to induce hypertrophy of the left liver.  
     - Interval (4–6 weeks): Continue systemic therapy; repeat imaging and volumetry to confirm FLR growth (>30 %).  
     - Stage 2: Right hepatectomy (including segments VI‑VIII) with or without reconstruction of the right hepatic vein, performed after confirming adequate hypertrophy.  
  3. If disease progresses despite chemotherapy – shift to second‑line systemic therapy (e.g., irinotecan‑based regimen with anti‑VEGF) and reassess for possible conversion; otherwise continue palliative treatment.  

- Peri‑operative chemotherapy  
  • Total peri‑operative chemotherapy duration of ~6 months (4 cycles pre‑op, 2–3 cycles post‑op) is recommended, consistent with EORTC‑40983 data.  
  • Post‑operative adjuvant FOLFOX (± anti‑EGFR) for 6 months, provided postoperative recovery is uneventful.  

- Multidisciplinary follow‑up  
  • Serial CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
  • Discuss any extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., pulmonary nodules) at each MDT meeting; consider simultaneous or staged pulmonary metastasectomy if lesions are limited and resectable.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Precise maximal diameters of each liver metastasis (especially the lesion contacting the right hepatic vein).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT/MRI volumetry).  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance to gauge hepatic reserve.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., pulmonary nodules) on staging scans.  
- Details of the primary sigmoid tumor’s local stage (obstruction, perforation) and whether it requires urgent resection.  
- Planned chemotherapy regimen (agents, dosing) and any prior exposure.  

These data are essential to finalize the surgical plan and to choose between a single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing approach versus a staged hepatectomy strategy.
