Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis. Current imaging shows extra‑hepatic disease (brain) that must be controlled before any curative‑intent liver surgery. Moreover, the burden of liver disease is not quantified (number, size, future liver remnant). According to the literature, limited extra‑hepatic disease that can be durably controlled (e.g., with stereotactic radiosurgery) may allow hepatic resection, but this requires prior treatment of the brain lesion and systemic therapy to assess tumor biology and to possibly downsize the liver disease. Therefore a prerequisite action (brain‑metastasis control and systemic chemotherapy) is needed before a definitive resection plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Immediate management of the cerebellar metastasis:  
   • If symptomatic or causing mass effect, stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) or microsurgical resection, followed by postoperative steroids as needed.  
   • Obtain postoperative MRI to confirm local control.  

2. Initiate systemic therapy for metastatic colorectal cancer:  
   • Preferred regimen: intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR according to RAS/BRAF status).  
   • Treat for 2–3 months (minimum 4–6 cycles) to assess disease biology and achieve possible downsizing of liver lesions.  

3. Restaging after systemic therapy:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with volumetric analysis to calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  
   • Repeat brain MRI to ensure continued control.  
   • Chest‑abdomen‑pelvis CT to evaluate any new extra‑hepatic sites.  

4. Decision point based on restaging:  
   • If liver disease responds sufficiently and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight ratio), plan a curative‑intent hepatic resection.  
   • For marginal FLR, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) to induce hypertrophy.  

5. Sequence of surgical procedures:  
   • Preferred “liver‑first” approach: perform hepatic resection after confirming adequate FLR and stable extra‑hepatic disease, thereby avoiding unnecessary colon surgery if systemic progression occurs.  
   • If the primary colon tumor is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or technically demanding (T4), address it first with right hemicolectomy (or extended resection) and then proceed to liver surgery after recovery.  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic and liver resection is feasible, consider simultaneous colon and liver resection only when the combined operative time and physiologic stress are acceptable (e.g., limited liver resection, good performance status).  

6. Post‑operative management:  
   • Continue systemic chemotherapy (adjuvant or maintenance) for at least 3–6 months, tailored to molecular profile and response.  
   • Consider postoperative radiotherapy to the cerebellar bed if surgical resection was performed.  
   • Regular surveillance with CEA, imaging of liver, chest, and brain every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Exact number, size, and distribution of liver metastases; volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
• Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) to select biologic agent.  
• Symptoms or complications related to the primary colon tumor (obstruction, bleeding).  
• Baseline liver function tests and bilirubin, albumin, coagulation profile.  
• Details of the cerebellar lesion (size, edema, symptomatic status) and planned local therapy.  
• Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodal treatment.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases associated with a cerebellar metastasis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (860 ng/mL). The presence of brain metastasis indicates advanced systemic dissemination and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Neurological priority (mandatory)
• Immediate neurosurgical and/or radiotherapy assessment of the cerebellar metastasis is required as the first therapeutic step.
• The objective is neurological control and symptom prevention.

B. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (860 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

C. Systemic therapy after neurological stabilization
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision once neurological status is stabilized.
• The objective is global disease control.

D. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and full-body imaging after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

E. Criteria for reconsidering liver-directed therapy (exceptional)
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare situation of complete neurological control and major hepatic response, which remains highly unlikely.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Neurological status and resectability of the cerebellar metastasis.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
D. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
E. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
F. Presence or absence of additional extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules. Current imaging does not define the size, number, anatomic location, or resectability of the lung lesions, nor does it provide a calculated future liver remnant (FLR). Both pieces of information are decisive for planning an R0 resection of all disease while preserving adequate hepatic and pulmonary function. Therefore the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and does not meet criteria for “Not resectable” because conversion strategies (systemic therapy, portal vein embolization, staged or combined resections) may render the disease operable once the missing data are clarified.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive conversion systemic therapy: 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX/FOLFIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild‑type status; consider adding bevacizumab only after the first 2 cycles if rapid tumor shrinkage is needed and surgical timing permits.  
- Re‑stage after 2–3 months with high‑resolution liver MRI and thin‑slice chest CT (or PET‑CT) to:  
   • Quantify response of liver lesions, measure each metastasis, and calculate FLR (target >30 % in normal liver or >0.5 % body weight).  
   • Define number, size, and anatomic distribution of pulmonary nodules; assess pulmonary function tests (FEV1, DLCO) to confirm surgical tolerance.  
- If liver disease remains extensive but FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the future resected hemiliver or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in one lobe + PVE; second stage: completion hepatectomy after hypertrophy). ALPPS may be an option if rapid hypertrophy is required and patient fitness permits.  
- If pulmonary nodules are ≤3 cm, peripheral, and limited in number, schedule curative‑intent pulmonary resection (wedge or segmentectomy) either simultaneously with liver resection (if operative risk acceptable) or in a staged fashion after hepatic surgery. If lesions are not surgically resectable but limited, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or percutaneous ablation as definitive local therapy.  
- Address the primary rectal tumor after hepatic (and pulmonary, if staged) control:  
   • For T4 disease involving adjacent organs, deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (45 Gy with capecitabine) followed by an interval of 6–8 weeks.  
   • Perform an abdominoperineal resection or low anterior resection with partial prostatectomy as required, ensuring negative margins (R0).  
- Post‑operative management: complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (continuing the same regimen or switching to maintenance anti‑EGFR) and consider hepatic arterial infusion pump or postoperative portal vein infusion if residual microscopic disease is suspected.  
- Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI of abdomen and chest CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed characteristics of pulmonary nodules (exact number, size, laterality, relationship to major bronchi/vessels).  
- Baseline pulmonary function tests (FEV1, DLCO) to gauge resection tolerance.  
- Precise dimensions of each liver metastasis and their relationship to major vascular/biliary structures.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume (CT‑volumetry or MRI).  
- Liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance) and performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
- Prior systemic therapy (none reported) and any response to initial chemotherapy if already given.  
- Details of rectal tumor involvement (distance from sphincter, invasion of prostate, need for radiotherapy).  
- Patient comorbidities (cardiovascular, renal, diabetes) that could affect major hepato‑pulmonary surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules in the context of a T4N2 rectal tumor and very high CEA (1250 ng/mL). The combination of extensive bilobar hepatic disease and extrahepatic pulmonary involvement reflects advanced systemic dissemination. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (1250 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare case of major response with significant reduction of both hepatic and pulmonary disease, allowing complete clearance of all sites.
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.

F. Pelvic management integration
• Plan rectal treatment (short-course radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy) according the MDT discussion if the primary tumor is symptomatic

G. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

H. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• If resection, analysis ofpathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

B. Characterization of pulmonary micronodules on chest CT.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary rectum tumor : detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the hepatic disease (segments IV, V, VIII) could be removed with an adequate future liver remnant, but resection cannot be undertaken now because (a) a confirmed right‑iliac bone metastasis represents extra‑hepatic disease that must be controlled (systemic therapy ± local bone treatment) before a curative‑intent liver operation, and (b) essential technical data (future liver remnant volume, liver function, performance status) are not provided to confirm that a safe hepatectomy is feasible.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated mCRC (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab) as first‑line; consider adding a bone‑targeted agent (zoledronic acid or denosumab) and local radiotherapy/SBRT to the right iliac lesion to achieve local control.  
• Re‑stage after 2–3 months of therapy with triphasic CT or MRI of the liver, PET‑CT for extra‑hepatic disease, and volumetric CT to calculate future liver remnant (target ≥ 30 % in chemotherapy‑naïve liver, ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑exposed).  
• If imaging shows ≥ 30 % reduction of liver lesions and the bone metastasis is stable or treated, proceed with a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   – Perform anatomical resection of segments IV, V, VIII (non‑major or combined segmentectomy) ensuring R0 margins and adequate FLR.  
   – If the primary left‑colon tumor remains in situ and is asymptomatic, schedule simultaneous colon resection (left hemicolectomy) after confirming that operative time and physiologic stress are acceptable; otherwise, resect the primary after hepatic recovery (staged).  
• Post‑hepatectomy, resume systemic chemotherapy (same regimen or switch to second‑line if progression) for at least 3 months, and deliver definitive local therapy to the bone lesion (SBRT or surgical fixation if symptomatic).  
• Continue surveillance with CT/MRI every 3 months for the first 2 years, monitoring CEA and bone imaging; consider adjuvant targeted therapy per evolving guidelines.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Baseline liver function tests and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
• Detailed characteristics of the bone metastasis (size, cortical involvement, pain, need for stabilization).  
• Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. in‑situ, symptomatic vs. asymptomatic).  
• Full staging of extra‑hepatic disease (chest imaging for pulmonary mets, PET‑CT for other sites).  
• Baseline tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9) and LDH.  
These data are required to finalize resectability and to tailor the peri‑operative plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with liver metastases in segments IV, V, and VIII associated with a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis in the context of a left colon cancer. The presence of osseous metastatic disease indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
•Perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Management of bone metastasis
• Integrate radiotherapy and/or orthopedic evaluation for the right iliac lesion depending on symptoms and fracture risk.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform periodic liver MRI and whole-body imaging to monitor response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Role of liver-directed therapy
• Liver surgery is not indicated unless an exceptional systemic response with control of bone disease occurs, which remains unlikely.

E. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

B. Extent and symptoms related to the iliac bone metastasis.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Classification: Not resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has eight bilobar liver metastases together with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis. Current consensus defines resectability primarily by the ability to achieve an R0 resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments, adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage and a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % (or >0.5 % liver/body‑weight ratio). Bilobar disease with eight lesions makes it unlikely that a sufficient FLR can be left, and the presence of moderate peritoneal disease represents extensive extra‑hepatic spread that is not amenable to curative resection in most cases. Consequently, curative‑intent hepatic and peritoneal surgery is excluded at this stage.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive systemic therapy as first line (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) pending molecular profiling (RAS/BRAF status, MSI‑H).  
- Obtain baseline high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and a CT‑ or PET‑CT‑based assessment of peritoneal disease to calculate a Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI).  
- Re‑image after 2–3 months of chemotherapy (or after 4–6 cycles) to evaluate radiologic response of both hepatic and peritoneal lesions (RECIST 1.1 and morphologic criteria).  
- If disease shows significant down‑staging (e.g., reduction in number/size of liver lesions, PCI ≤10, no new extra‑hepatic sites) and a satisfactory FLR can be projected (≥30 % after potential portal vein embolisation), discuss conversion to a staged hepatic approach:  
   • Consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) to hypertrophy the future liver remnant, followed by a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS if hypertrophy is adequate and liver function remains acceptable.  
   • Simultaneous or sequential resection of the primary colon tumor should be planned based on symptomatology (obstruction, bleeding) and response to chemotherapy; a colon‑first approach is preferred for right‑sided T4 lesions unless urgent hepatic control is needed.  
- If peritoneal disease remains extensive (PCI > 15) or liver disease does not become resectable, continue systemic therapy with possible incorporation of targeted agents (anti‑EGFR for RAS‑wildtype) or immunotherapy (for MSI‑H). Consider enrollment in a clinical trial or palliative liver‑directed therapies (radiofrequency ablation, selective internal radiation therapy) for symptom control.  
- Throughout treatment, maintain multidisciplinary review, monitor CEA trends, and assess performance status and liver function before any surgical attempt.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF mutation status, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
- Patient’s ECOG performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Detailed liver function tests and baseline liver volumetry to calculate the future liver remnant.  
- Precise peritoneal disease burden (PCI score) and whether any lesions are resectable or amenable to HIPEC.  
- Presence of symptoms from the primary colon tumor (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
- Prior exposure to chemotherapy or radiotherapy (none reported yet).  
- Baseline imaging reports (size of each hepatic lesion, vascular involvement, proximity to major hepatic veins/portal structures).  
- Nutritional status and serum albumin.  

These data are essential to refine the conversion strategy and to determine whether a curative‑intent surgical plan can become feasible after systemic therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
C. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
E. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
F. Patient’s performance status for staged surgical procedures.
